17592186130960}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "008f670b-b77a-5939-9c4f-8602d138cc7d" :question/math-academy-id "q-162377" :question/problem "Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $r(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,k$ for $t\in [-1,1).$
Given that $F(x,y,z)=x\,i+y\,k,$ evaluate the integral

$$
{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t),\,y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t),\,z=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t).
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i+y\,k \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\,k \\  & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,i-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k)\cdot (\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,i-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)-0\cdot \pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t) \\  & =\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+\pi {cos}^{2}⁡(\pi t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+\pi {cos}^{2}⁡(\pi t))\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+\frac{\pi }{2}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t)))\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t)}{2}+\frac{\pi t}{2}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t)}{4}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =0+\frac{\pi }{2}+0-(0-\frac{\pi }{2}+0) \\  & =\pi \end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "cb01237b-4d73-5b10-94f4-c0c4f3fdada5" :step/next {:db/id 17592186521583}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c97d45ae-ae12-5c14-924c-d56fbb9046f0" :answer/type {:db/id \end{aligned}

$$

$$

![](images/bf/bfe277aaf4c57d73d2649d8ade756cf04411ba23a049a6e1283d18c3e711a7fa.png)

The function is not defined for

$$
x\leq 2
$$

Therefore,

$$
\lim_\limits{x \to 2^{-}} \ln (x-2) = \textrm{DNE}
$$

However, the function is defined for $x\gt 2$. Therefore,

$$
\lim_\limits{x \to 2^{+}} \ln (x-2) = -\infty
$$

$$
\lim_\limits{x \to 2} \ln (x-2) = \textrm{DNE}

From the graph, we see that

$$
\lim_{x\to3}\log_2{x} = \log_2{3}\approx 1.58
$$

For logarithmic functions, the limit at a point is equal to the value of the function at that point, so for any base $b \gt 1$ we have

$$
\lim_{x\to c}\log_b{x} = \log_b{c}
$$

Remember that logarithms are only defined for positive inputs $x\gt 0$, so we must have $c>0$. ![](images/30/30a66b56ea1422fc61941d22aedbbf3f17e06810e66e6590490bd4b7188fd361.png)

As $x$ gets larger and larger, the curve increases without bound. So, we have

$$
\lim_{x\to\infty} \log_2{x}= \infty
$$

The curve is not defined for

$$
x\leq 0
$$

but as $x$ approaches zero from the right the curve *decreases* without bound. So

$$
\lim_{x\to0^+}\log_2{x} = -\infty
$$

Also, note that

$$
\lim_{x\to0^-}\log_2{x} = \textrm{DNE},\qquad\qquad \lim_{x\to0}\log_2{x} = \textrm{DNE}
$$

These properties are true for logarithms of any base $b\gt 1$." :tutorial/id #uuid "12a53922-65d6-5add-afe1-cbf5afcf1f1e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2892 :tutorial/title "Infinite Limits and Limits at $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ Given that the eigenvalues of ${A}^{T}A$ are $5,$ $3,$ and $0,$ find the length of the ellipse's semi-major axis." :question/worked-solution "The matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$

Since the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ is $5,$ we obtain

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}=5\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=\sqrt{5}.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is $\sqrt{5}.$"} {:db/id 17592186162364 :question/id #uuid "7f4eb209-024e-54c1-8d3d-a6d7fb7fadd8" :question/math-academy-id "q-139491"} {:db/id Given that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A,$ which of the following is an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $25$ of ${A}^{T}A?$" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix. Let 

$$
\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\,…,{v}_{n}\}
$$

be an *orthonormal* basis of ${R}^{n}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A$ with corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}\ge …\ge {\lambda }_{n}.
$$

Then,

- ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{1},$

- ${\sigma }_{2}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{2},$

- $⋯$

In our example, we see that

:topic/math-academy-id 3131} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186163048 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163315 :tutorial/content "Let's suppose we are given the matrix

![](images/18/18f57c05cb79918e17401427e3419648791562a5d38116582e0d396e20db1069.svg)

Then, the corresponding linear transformation 

$$
\mathbf x \mapsto A \mathbf x
$$

maps the unit circle $\big\{ \mathbf x \, | \, \|\mathbf x\|=1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb R^2$ onto an ellipse $\big\{ A\mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2,$ as shown below. 

![](images/c1/c163f7714d0e2045db37438b7ea66a2dc8ac92cfbe309a0d24c898bbfac8c295.png)

 

How can we find the maximum possible value of $\|A \mathbf x\|?$ Geometrically, this is equivalent to finding the semi-major axis of our ellipse.

![](images/86/866052291b0d7a416988c0c42fa99eec1d1bfd3b1344cf3cf2eb0a09457ae38d.png)

First, we note the following:

- The value of $\mathbf x$ that maximizes $||A\mathbf x||$ also maximizes $||A\mathbf x||^2.$

- If $\mathbf v$ is a column vector, then $||\mathbf v||^2 = \mathbf v^T \mathbf v\mathbin{:}$

Therefore, we can re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $A\mathbf{x}$ on our ellipse as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x\end{aligned}
$$

  

Note that $\mathbf{x}^T (A^T A) \mathbf{x}$ is a quadratic form with the matrix $A^T A.$ Therefore, the maximum value of this quadratic form for $\| \mathbf{x} \| =1$ equals the largest eigenvalue of the matrix $A^T A.$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & 6 \\ 6 & 10\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^TA\mathbin{:}$  

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}10-\lambda  & 6 \\ 6 & 10-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )^{2}-36 & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )^{2} & =36 \\ 10-\lambda  & =\pm 6 \\ \lambda  & =4,\,16\end{aligned}
$$

Since the largest eigenvalue of $A^T A$ is $16,$ we obtain

$$
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \|^2 \big\} = 16
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \| \big\} = \sqrt{16} = 4.
$$

 

Therefore, the length of the semi-major axis of our ellipse equals $4.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b6f73158-b78c-5262-bb9d-a957e3f79fa3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6133 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} Then, $A^T A$ is always a symmetric, positive semi-definite matrix. In particular, $A^TA$ can be orthogonally diagonalized, and its eigenvalues are non-negative real numbers.

The **singular values** of  $A$ are defined as the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T A.$ The $i$th singular value of $A$ is denoted $\sigma_i\mathbin{:}$

- $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{\lambda_1}$

- $\sigma_2 = \sqrt{\lambda_2}$

- $\sigma_3 = \sqrt{\lambda_3}$

$\:\vdots$

- $\sigma_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}$

We usually list the singular values in *decreasing* order. 

Now, we know that $A^TA$ is orthogonally diagonalizable. Therefore, if

$$
\left\{\mathbf v_1, \mathbf v_2\,\ldots, \mathbf v_n\right\}
$$

is an *orthonormal* basis of $\mathbb R^n$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A^T}{A}$ with the corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
\lambda_1\geq \lambda_2\geq \ldots \geq \lambda_n,
$$

then it can be shown that

- $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{\lambda_1}$ is the length of $A\mathbf v_1,$

- $\sigma_2 = \sqrt{\lambda_2}$ is the length of $A\mathbf v_2,$

$\:\vdots$

- $\sigma_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}$ is the length of $A\mathbf v_n.$

Furthermore:

- $\sigma_1$ is the maximum value of $||A\mathbf x||$ over all *unit* vectors $\mathbf x,$ and is attained on the unit eigenvector $\mathbf v_1$

- $\sigma_2$ is the maximum value of $||A\mathbf x||$ over all *unit* vectors $\mathbf x$ that are orthogonal to $\mathbf v_1,$ and is attained on the unit eigenvector $\mathbf v_2$

- $\sigma_3$ is the maximum value of $||A\mathbf x||$ over all *unit* vectors $\mathbf x$ that are orthogonal to $\mathbf v_1$ *and* $\mathbf v_2,$ and is attained on the unit eigenvector $\mathbf v_3$

$\:\vdots$

- $\sigma_n$ is the maximum value of $||A\mathbf x||$ over all *unit* vectors $\mathbf x$ that are orthogonal to $\mathbf v_1,\mathbf v_2,\ldots,\mathbf v_{n-1},$ and is attained on the unit eigenvector $\mathbf v_n$

the eigenvalues of $A^TA$ are $\lambda_1=16$ and $\lambda_2=4.$ It's easy to show that the corresponding unit eigenvectors of $A^T A$ are 

![](images/7c/7c44b67b766ea8385f4d7780523ee560bd3e215a0cee42db9baf208da471ccdd.svg) 

The singular values of $A$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{16}=4, \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting all of this information together gives us the following diagram. 

![](images/23/238f4ae60c783dd786476a339f012ef1b4ca82bcac7aa3f3ef4445726938ef3a.png)

Then, $A^T A$ is always a symmetric, positive semi-definite matrix. In particular, $A^TA$ can be orthogonally diagonalized, and its eigenvalues are non-negative real numbers.

The **singular values** of  $A$ are defined as the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T A.$ The $i$th singular value of $A$ is denoted $\sigma_i\mathbin{:}$

- $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{\lambda_1}$

- $\sigma_2 = \sqrt{\lambda_2}$

- $\sigma_3 = \sqrt{\lambda_3}$

$\:\vdots$

- $\sigma_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}$

We usually list the singular values in *decreasing* order. 

Now, we know that $A^TA$ is orthogonally diagonalizable. Therefore, if

$$
\left\{\mathbf v_1, \mathbf v_2\,\ldots, \mathbf v_n\right\}
$$

is an *orthonormal* basis of $\mathbb R^n$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A^T}{A}$ with the corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
\lambda_1\geq \lambda_2\geq \ldots \geq \lambda_n,
$$

then it can be shown that

- $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{\lambda_1}$ is the length of $A\mathbf v_1,$

- $\sigma_2 = \sqrt{\lambda_2}$ is the length of $A\mathbf v_2,$

$\:\vdots$

- $\sigma_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}$ is the length of $A\mathbf v_n.$

Furthermore:

- $\sigma_1$ is the maximum value of $||A\mathbf x||$ over all *unit* vectors $\mathbf x,$ and is attained on the unit eigenvector $\mathbf v_1$

- $\sigma_2$ is the maximum value of $||A\mathbf x||$ over all *unit* vectors $\mathbf x$ that are orthogonal to $\mathbf v_1,$ and is attained on the unit eigenvector $\mathbf v_2$

- $\sigma_3$ is the maximum value of $||A\mathbf x||$ over all *unit* vectors $\mathbf x$ that are orthogonal to $\mathbf v_1$ *and* $\mathbf v_2,$ and is attained on the unit eigenvector $\mathbf v_3$

$\:\vdots$

- $\sigma_n$ is the maximum value of $||A\mathbf x||$ over all *unit* vectors $\mathbf x$ that are orthogonal to $\mathbf v_1,\mathbf v_2,\ldots,\mathbf v_{n-1},$ and is attained on the unit eigenvector $\mathbf v_n$

Let's take a look at a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "f470bdb6-fa79-595c-beba-f8242d4426bd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6134 :tutorial/title "The Singular Values of a Matrix"} {:db/id 17592186163056 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163320 :tutorial/content "We've seen that for the matrix $A,$ given by

:question/worked-solution "The matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The square roots of the eigenvalues of ${A}^{T}A$ are called the *singular values* of $A.$ Since the largest singular value of $A$ is ${\sigma }_{1}=8,$ the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ must be ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}={8}^{2}.$ So, we obtain that

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}={8}^{2}\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=8.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is ${\sigma }_{1}=8.$"} :step/id #uuid "9ba70a3c-71a0-5cb6-a4db-f475dda224da" :step/next {:db/id 17592186524078}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The square roots of the eigenvalues of ${A}^{T}A$ are called the *singular values* of $A.$ Since the largest singular value of $A$ is ${\sigma }_{1}=8,$ the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ must be ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}={8}^{2}.$ So, we obtain that

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}={8}^{2}\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=8.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is ${\sigma }_{1}=8.$"} :step/id #uuid "417441ef-0974-5094-9fdd-ef33aedcf95b" :step/next {:db/id 17592186559967}} {:db/id 17592186559967 :step/content {:db/id 17592186400763 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "72d8c257-9208-59a3-b8ef-e84226b5d7cc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$5$ and $3$" :db/id 17592186400765} {:answer/id #uuid "c56b5625-8f3f-5546-bd45-82c8dcf4f2c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$25$ and $9$" :db/id 17592186400766} {:answer/id #uuid "9f361d5f-db40-531a-8f20-5389f05b015d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$\sqrt{7}$ and $\sqrt{3}$" :db/id 17592186400767} {:answer/id #uuid "c82a5223-3bd0-5bad-9e6b-edd5899707f1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$11$ and $7$" :db/id 17592186400768} {:answer/id #uuid "e7a6a4f9-ba6e-5a5b-9c4a-a88207909379" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$6$ and $4$" :db/id 17592186400769}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186400765} :answer-field/id #uuid "4dac3c89-e776-5135-b836-fafd4c581933" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186400764}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "925e17f0-1f91-564c-b150-3d5633a84c6e" :question/math-academy-id "q-139546" :question/problem "![](images/6d/6df3639cb222756221803446ebc735cf1e7cbcf4a922ed7fce835c0c44fb9aa1.png)

- ${\sigma }_{2}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{2},$

$$
ABC \sim PQR
$$

$$
\angle A \cong \angle P, \qquad \angle B \cong \angle Q, \qquad \angle C \cong \angle R.
$$

$$
k = \dfrac{AB}{PQ}= \dfrac{BC}{QR} =  \dfrac{AC}{PR},
$$

More precisely, two polygons are similar if the following conditions hold:

1\. Their corresponding angles are congruent.

2\. The ratios of the lengths of their corresponding sides are all equal.

To demonstrate, let's consider the triangles $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle EFG$ below.

![](images/23/233fcb591a81d9ee6eef3caf1f4df0f0e959a18144177e89d5f0ac88c94525f4.png)

From the figure above, we see that the corresponding angles are congruent:

$$
\angle A \cong \angle E, \qquad \angle B \cong \angle F, \qquad \angle C \cong \angle G.
$$

We also need to check whether the ratios of the corresponding sides are the same. That is, we have to check whether

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{AB}{EF} & =\frac{BC}{FG}=\frac{AC}{EG}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the lengths of the sides, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{AB}{EF} & =\frac{6}{12}=\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{BC}{FG} & =\frac{4}{8}=\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{AC}{EG} & =\frac{5}{10}=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

The ratios are the same. Therefore, we conclude that the triangles $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle EFG$ are similar. The common ratio of the sides, $\dfrac{1}{2},$ is called the **similarity ratio**.

To express mathematically that the triangles $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle EFG$ are similar, we write

$$
\triangle ABC \sim \triangle EFG.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "d16f60d4-ecf1-552e-82e5-d75e3cee2d89" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2312 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "64268339-5582-581d-80ef-13e6ca1ae5d8" :step/math-academy-id Two-Dimensional Space"}] :question/problem "Let $L$ be the line with equation $y=5+3x$ in $\mathbb{R}^2.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. $L$ contains the zero-vector

II. $L$ is closed under vector addition

III. $L$ is closed under scalar multiplication

IV. $L$ is **not** a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2$" :question/worked-solution "Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0 \cdot \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ for any vector $\mathbf{v}$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

Notice that $L$ contains vectors of the form 

![](images/72/7202d8cbdd95abf0bce85cd66490b29abe5737259def341fcb3202a06c6140a0.svg)

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is false. The coordinates of the zero-vector do not satisfy the equation $y=5+3x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =5+3x \\ (0) & =5+3(0) \\ 0 & =5\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Let, for example, ![](images/9b/9b7dd489c2bd902529876d678dd3e21d3503f1d42aafba6aa6b3c40dad8f61da.svg) and ![](images/91/911a47012bbfefca8e19f14c023c3924a5e6e02470d6825ad8e4525816bcf2a2.svg) from $L.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0+(-1) \\ 5+2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 7\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 
However, ![](images/db/dbbce97422b8e84b3408bc64d43a250bcba2bd5f2ba5ea5a6aa282e884fa8750.svg) since substituting the coordinates into the equation $y=5+3x$ gives the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =5+3x \\ 7 & =5+3(-1) \\ 7 & =2\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $\mathbf{0} \not\in L,$ this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement IV is true. Since statements II and III are false, $L$ is *not* a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "IV only.""} {:db/id 17592186048499} {:db/id 17592186049716} {:db/id 17592186050367} {:db/id 17592186120145 :question/id #uuid "44d1d34b-4b40-5331-8b03-073462e9a684" :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Let $L$ be the line with equation $y=-x$ in ${R}^{2}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $L$ contains the zero-vector

- **II.** $L$ is closed under vector addition

- **III.** $L$ is closed under scalar multiplication

- **IV.** $L$ is a subspace of ${R}^{2}$" :question/worked-solution "Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

Notice that $L$ contains vectors of the form 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ -x\end{bmatrix},\,x\in R.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is true. The coordinates of the zero-vector satisfy the equation $y=-x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-x \\ (0) & =-(0) \\ 0 & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Let, for example, $a=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ -a\end{bmatrix}\in L$ and $b=\begin{bmatrix}b \\ -b\end{bmatrix}\in L.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =\begin{bmatrix}a \\ -a\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}b \\ -b\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}a+b \\ (-a)+(-b)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}a+b \\ -(a+b)\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $y=-x.$ Therefore, $a+b\in L.$

- Statement III is true. Let, for example, $a=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ -a\end{bmatrix}\in L$ and $k\in R.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}k\cdot a & =k\cdot \begin{bmatrix}a \\ -a\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}ka \\ k(-a)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}ka \\ -(ka)\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $y=-x.$ Therefore, $k\cdot a\in L.$

- Statement IV is true. Since statements II and III are true, $L$ must be a subspace of ${R}^{2}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "All the statements are true.""} {:db/id 17592186275358 :question/id #uuid "238a8f80-b240-55d1-a1f3-be7bf8e77e18" :question/math-academy-id "q-156624" 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Let $L$ be the line with equation $x=2y-1$ in ${R}^{2}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $L$ contains the zero-vector
- **II.** $L$ is closed under vector addition
- **III.** $L$ is closed under scalar multiplication
- **IV.** $L$ is **not** a subspace of ${R}^{2}$" :question/worked-solution "Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

Notice that $L$ contains vectors of the form 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2y-1 \\ y\end{bmatrix},\,y\in R.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is false. The coordinates of the zero-vector do not satisfy the equation $x=2y-1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2y-1 \\ (0) & =2(0)-1 \\ 0 & =-1\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Let, for example, $a=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ and $b=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ from $L.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1+1 \\ 0+1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 
However, $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\notin L$ since substituting the coordinates into the equation, we obtain the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2y-1 \\ (0) & =2(1)-1 \\ 0 & =1\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $0\notin L,$ this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement IV is true. Since statements II and III are false, $L$ is *not* a subspace of ${R}^{2}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "IV only.""} {:db/id 17592186275359 :question/id #uuid "f3a8da8b-2b40-54c1-8d4a-0bb7a1d10698" :question/math-academy-id "q-156628"} {:db/id 17592186275361 :question/id :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Let $L$ be the line with equation $4x=2y$ in ${R}^{2}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $L$ contains the zero-vector
- **II.** $L$ is closed under vector addition
- **III.** $L$ is closed under scalar multiplication
- **IV.** $L$ is **not** a subspace of ${R}^{2}$" :question/worked-solution "Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

Notice that $L$ contains vectors of the form 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ 2x\end{bmatrix},\,x\in R.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is true. The coordinates of the zero-vector satisfy the equation $4x=2y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4x & =2y \\ 4(0) & =2(0) \\ 0 & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Let, for example, $a=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 2a\end{bmatrix}\in L$ and $b=\begin{bmatrix}b \\ 2b\end{bmatrix}\in L.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 2a\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}b \\ 2b\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}a+b \\ 2a+2b\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}a+b \\ 2(a+b)\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $4x=2y.$ Therefore, $a+b\in L.$

- Statement III is true. Let, for example, $a=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 2a\end{bmatrix}\in L$ and $k\in R.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}k\cdot a & =k\cdot \begin{bmatrix}a \\ 2a\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}ka \\ k(2a)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}ka \\ 2(ka)\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

 
which satisfies the condition $4x=2y.$ Therefore, $k\cdot a\in L.$

- Statement IV is false. Since statements II and III are true, $L$ must be a subspace of ${R}^{2}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186119927 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119501 :question/id #uuid "d0d76105-c49e-5cf8-af57-bd74989e895b" are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $L$ contains the zero-vector

- **II.** $L$ is closed under vector addition

- **III.** $L$ is closed under scalar multiplication

- **IV.** $L$ is **not** a subspace of ${R}^{3}$" :question/worked-solution "Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is false. The direction vector of the line $L$ is 

$$
d=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -4 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -6 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

This means that the vector equation of the line is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -6 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

for $t\in R,$ and the corresponding Cartesian equation is 

$$
\frac{x+2}{5}=\frac{y-2}{-6}=\frac{z+2}{4}.
$$

But this line does not pass through the origin since 

$$
\frac{(0)+2}{5}\ne \frac{(0)-2}{-6}\ne \frac{(0)+2}{4}.\,\times 
$$

- Statement II is false. Let's consider the vectors $\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}$ and $\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -4 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}$ from $L$ (the position vectors of the given points). Then,

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -4 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

However, the point $(1,-2,0)$ does not belong to $L$ since

$$
\frac{(1)+2}{5}\ne \frac{(-2)-2}{-6}\ne \frac{(0)+2}{4}.\,\times 
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $0\notin L,$ this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement IV is true. Since statements II and III are false, $L$ is *not* a subspace of ${R}^{3}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "IV only.""} {:db/id 17592186120151 :question/id #uuid "fe544997-b5f0-5f74-9a6d-c604c1790f93" :question/math-academy-id "q-156679"} {:db/id 17592186275363 :question/id :answer-field/key "IV" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186465172}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Let $L$ be the line in ${R}^{3}$ that passes through the points $(0,0,0)$ and $(2,1,-1).$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $L$ contains the zero-vector

- **II.** $L$ is closed under vector addition

- **III.** $L$ is closed under scalar multiplication

- **IV.** $L$ is **not** a subspace of ${R}^{3}$" :question/worked-solution "Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

First, note that the direction vector of the line $L$ is 

$$
d=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

This means that the vector equation of the line is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2t \\ t \\ -t\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

for $t\in R,$ and the corresponding Cartesian equation is 

$$
\frac{x}{2}=y=-z.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is true. Indeed, from the definition of $L$ we have that the point $(0,0,0)$ is in $L.$

- Statement II is true. Let, for example, $a=\begin{bmatrix}2a \\ a \\ -a\end{bmatrix}\in L$ and $b=\begin{bmatrix}2b \\ b \\ -b\end{bmatrix}\in L.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =\begin{bmatrix}2a \\ a \\ -a\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2b \\ b \\ -b\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2a+2b \\ a+b \\ (-a)+(-b)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2(a+b) \\ a+b \\ -(a+b)\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the conditions $\frac{x}{2}=y=-z.$ Therefore, $a+b\in L.$

- Statement III is true. Let, for example, $a=\begin{bmatrix}2a \\ a \\ -a\end{bmatrix}\in L$ and $k\in R.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}k\cdot a & =k\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2a \\ a \\ -a\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}k(2a) \\ ka \\ k(-a)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2(ka) \\ ka \\ -(ka)\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the conditions $\frac{x}{2}=y=-z.$ Therefore, $k\cdot a\in L.$

- Statement IV is false. Since statements II and III are true, $L$ is a subspace of ${R}^{3}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186275391 :question/id #uuid "f036c2d4-285c-5c5e-a300-6732346f17c0" :question/math-academy-id "q-157374" 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Let $L$ be the line in ${R}^{3}$ that passes through the points $(0,0,0)$ and $(1,-2,3).$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $L$ contains the zero-vector

- **II.** $L$ is closed under vector addition

- **III.** $L$ is closed under scalar multiplication

- **IV.** $L$ is a subspace of ${R}^{3}$" :question/worked-solution "Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

First, note that the direction vector of the line $L$ is 

$$
d=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

This means that the vector equation of the line is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}t \\ -2t \\ 3t\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

for $t\in R,$ and the corresponding Cartesian equation is 

$$
x=-\frac{y}{2}=\frac{z}{3}.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is true. Indeed, from the definition of $L$ we have that the point $(0,0,0)$ is in $L.$

- Statement II is true. Let, for example, $a=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ -2a \\ 3a\end{bmatrix}\in L$ and $b=\begin{bmatrix}b \\ -2b \\ 3b\end{bmatrix}\in L.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =\begin{bmatrix}a \\ -2a \\ 3a\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}b \\ -2b \\ 3b\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}a+b \\ (-2a)+(-2b) \\ 3a+3b\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}a+b \\ -2(a+b) \\ 3(a+b)\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the conditions $x=-\frac{y}{2}=\frac{z}{3}.$ Therefore, $a+b\in L.$

- Statement III is true. Let, for example, $a=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ -2a \\ 3a\end{bmatrix}\in L$ and $k\in R.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}k\cdot a & =k\cdot \begin{bmatrix}a \\ -2a \\ 3a\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}ka \\ k(-2a) \\ k(3a)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}ka \\ -2(ka) \\ 3(ka)\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the conditions $x=-\frac{y}{2}=\frac{z}{3}.$ Therefore, $k\cdot a\in L.$

- Statement IV is true. Since statements II and III are true, $L$ is a subspace of ${R}^{3}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "All the statements are true.""} {:db/id 17592186275392 :question/id #uuid "fec918c0-b48b-51d4-9fda-9d6b7c9058ec" :question/math-academy-id "q-157375"} {:db/id are true?
- **I.** $L$ contains the zero-vector
- **II.** $L$ is closed under vector addition
- **III.** $L$ is closed under scalar multiplication
- **IV.** $L$ is a subspace of ${R}^{3}$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is false. The direction vector of the line $L$ is 

$$
d=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

This means that the vector equation of the line is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

for $t\in R,$ and the corresponding Cartesian equation is 

$$
x-1=\frac{y-1}{-2}=z-1.
$$

But this line does not pass through the origin since 

$$
(0)-1\ne \frac{(0)-1}{-2}\ne (0)-1.\,\times 
$$

- Statement II is false. Let's consider the vectors $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ and $\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}$ from $L$ (the position vectors of the given points). Then,

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

However, the point $(3,0,3)$ does not belong to $L$ since

$$
(3)-1\ne \frac{(0)-1}{-2}\ne (3)-1.\,\times 
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $0\notin L,$ this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement IV is false. Since statements II and III are false, $L$ is *not* a subspace of ${R}^{3}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true.""} {:db/id 17592186275394 :question/id #uuid "21a6de96-a543-5af1-a71d-fa101cbb68c3" :question/math-academy-id "q-157392"} {:db/id are true?
- **I.** $L$ contains the zero-vector
- **II.** $L$ is closed under vector addition
- **III.** $L$ is closed under scalar multiplication
- **IV.** $L$ is a subspace of ${R}^{3}$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is false.The direction vector of the line $L$ is 

$$
d=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

This means that the vector equation of the line is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

for $t\in R,$ and the corresponding Cartesian equation is 

$$
x=\frac{y+1}{3}=\frac{z-2}{-2}.
$$

But this line does not pass through the origin since 

$$
(0)\ne \frac{(0)+1}{3}\ne \frac{(0)-2}{-2}.\,\times 
$$

- Statement II is false. Let's consider the vectors $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}$ and $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ from $L$ (the position vectors of the given points). Then,

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

However, the point $(1,1,2)$ does not belong to $L$ since

$$
(1)\ne \frac{(1)+1}{3}\ne \frac{(2)-2}{-2}.\,\times 
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $0\notin L,$ this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement IV is false. Since statements II and III are false, $L$ is *not* a subspace of ${R}^{3}.$

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

for $t\in R,$ and the corresponding Cartesian equation is 

$$
\frac{x-1}{-2}=\frac{y+1}{2}=\frac{z-2}{-1}.
$$

But this line does not pass through the origin since 

$$
\frac{(0)-1}{-2}=\frac{(0)+1}{2}\ne \frac{(0)-2}{-1}\,\times 
$$

- Statement II is false. Let's consider the vectors $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}$ and $\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ from $L$ (the position vectors of the given points). Then,

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

However, the point $(0,0,3)$ does not belong to $L$ since

$$
\frac{(0)-1}{-2}=\frac{(0)+1}{2}\ne -(3)+2.\,\times 
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $0\notin L,$ this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0 \cdot \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ for any vector $\mathbf{v}$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

$$
\begin{aligned}x+4y-3z & =2 \\ (0)+4(0)-3(0) & =2 \\ 0 & =2\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Let's consider ![](images/d0/d0cf195a83c36291bae09c62f542449734d024fadae23b99cecbb4507f03c430.svg) and ![](images/13/13f8e15407cd0dbdfc080f19f906df1ed4bf984635cb2eb30b01f95d50695d53.svg) Then

$$

However, $\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ does not belong to $\Pi$ since 

$$
\begin{aligned}x+4y-3z & =2 \\ (3)+4(1)-3(1) & =2 \\ 4 & =2\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $\mathbf{0} \not\in \Pi,$ this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement IV is true. Since statements II and III are false, $\Pi$ is *not* a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3.$

:answer-field/key "IV" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186449266}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Let $Π$ be the plane with equation $z=x-y$ in ${R}^{3}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $Π$ contains the zero-vector
- **II.** $Π$ is closed under vector addition
- **III.** $Π$ is closed under scalar multiplication
- **IV.** $Π$ is **not** a subspace of ${R}^{3}$" :question/worked-solution "Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

Notice that $Π$ contains vectors of the form 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ x-y\end{bmatrix},\,x,y\in R.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is true. The coordinates of the zero-vector satisfy the equation $z=x-y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =x-y \\ (0) & =(0)-(0) \\ 0 & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Let, for example, $a=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} \\ {a}_{1}-{a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\in Π$ and $b=\begin{bmatrix}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2} \\ {b}_{1}-{b}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\in Π.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} \\ {a}_{1}-{a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2} \\ {b}_{1}+{b}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1}+{b}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}+{b}_{2} \\ ({a}_{1}-{a}_{2})+({b}_{1}-{b}_{2})\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1}+{b}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}+{b}_{2} \\ ({a}_{1}+{b}_{1})-({a}_{2}+{b}_{2})\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $z=x-y.$ Therefore, $a+b\in Π.$

- Statement III is true. Let, for example, $a=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} \\ {a}_{1}-{a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\in Π$ and $k\in R.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}k\cdot a & =k\cdot \begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} \\ {a}_{1}-{a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}k{a}_{1} \\ k{a}_{2} \\ k({a}_{1}-{a}_{2})\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}k{a}_{1} \\ k{a}_{2} \\ k{a}_{1}-k{a}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $z=x-y.$ Therefore, $k\cdot a\in Π.$

- Statement IV is false. Since statements II and III are true, $Π$ must be a subspace of ${R}^{3}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186275364 :question/id #uuid "36959921-7ebb-5f39-a723-592fbf72eec8" :question/math-academy-id "q-156728"} {:db/id 17592186275395 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Let $Π$ be the plane with equation $z=2x-y$ in ${R}^{3}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $Π$ contains the zero-vector

- **II.** $Π$ is closed under vector addition

- **III.** $Π$ is closed under scalar multiplication

- **IV.** $Π$ is **not** a subspace of ${R}^{3}$" :question/worked-solution "Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

Notice that $Π$ contains vectors of the form 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ 2x-y\end{bmatrix},\,x,y\in R.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is true. The coordinates of the zero-vector satisfy the equation $z=2x-y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =2x-y \\ (0) & =2(0)-(0) \\ 0 & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Let, for example, $a=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} \\ 2{a}_{1}-{a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\in Π$ and $b=\begin{bmatrix}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2} \\ 2{b}_{1}-{b}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\in Π.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} \\ 2{a}_{1}-{a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2} \\ 2{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1}+{b}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}+{b}_{2} \\ (2{a}_{1}-{a}_{2})+(2{b}_{1}-{b}_{2})\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1}+{b}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}+{b}_{2} \\ 2({a}_{1}+{b}_{1})-({a}_{2}+{b}_{2})\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $z=2x-y.$ Therefore, $a+b\in Π.$

- Statement III is true. Let, for example, $a=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} \\ 2{a}_{1}-{a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\in Π$ and $k\in R.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}k\cdot a & =k\cdot \begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} \\ 2{a}_{1}-{a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}k{a}_{1} \\ k{a}_{2} \\ k(2{a}_{1}-{a}_{2})\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}k{a}_{1} \\ k{a}_{2} \\ 2(k{a}_{1})-k{a}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $z=2x-y.$ Therefore, $k\cdot a\in Π.$

- Statement IV is false. Since statements II and III are true, $Π$ must be a subspace of ${R}^{3}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186275396 :question/id #uuid "19a5b6b6-a775-5cf8-81ee-dfec54297bbf" :question/math-academy-id "q-157464" Select all that apply.

- **I.** $Π$ contains the zero-vector

- **II.** $Π$ is closed under vector addition

- **III.** $Π$ is closed under scalar multiplication

- **IV.** $Π$ is a subspace of ${R}^{3}$" :question/worked-solution "Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

Notice that $Π$ contains vectors of the form 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ x+2y\end{bmatrix},\,x,y\in R.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is true. The coordinates of the zero-vector satisfy the equation $z=x+2y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =x+2y \\ (0) & =(0)+2(0) \\ 0 & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Let, for example, $a=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} \\ {a}_{1}+2{a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\in Π$ and $b=\begin{bmatrix}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2} \\ {b}_{1}+2{b}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\in Π.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} \\ {a}_{1}+2{a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2} \\ {b}_{1}+2{b}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1}+{b}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}+{b}_{2} \\ ({a}_{1}+2{a}_{2})+({b}_{1}+2{b}_{2})\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1}+{b}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}+{b}_{2} \\ ({a}_{1}+{b}_{1})+2({a}_{2}+{b}_{2})\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $z=x+2y.$ Therefore, $a+b\in Π.$

- Statement III is true. Let, for example, $a=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} \\ {a}_{1}+2{a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\in Π$ and $k\in R.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}k\cdot a & =k\cdot \begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} \\ {a}_{1}+2{a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}k{a}_{1} \\ k{a}_{2} \\ k({a}_{1}+2{a}_{2})\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}k{a}_{1} \\ k{a}_{2} \\ k{a}_{1}+2(k{a}_{2})\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $z=x+2y.$ Therefore, $k\cdot a\in Π.$

- Statement IV is true. Since statements II and III are true, the plane $Π$ must be a subspace of ${R}^{3}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "All the statements are true.""} {:db/id 17592186275397 :question/id #uuid "70407f65-cb23-502b-8caa-ecb6f34e8d13" :question/math-academy-id "q-157468"} {:db/id - A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

Notice that $Π$ contains vectors of the form 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1+2y-z \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix},\,y,z\in R.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is false. The line does not pass through the origin since

$$
\begin{aligned}x-2y+z & =1 \\ (0)-2(0)+(0) & =1 \\ 0 & =1\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Let's consider $a=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\in Π$ and $b=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\in Π.$ Then 

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1+0 \\ 0+0 \\ 0+1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

However, $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ does not belong to $Π$ since 

$$
\begin{aligned}x-2y+z & =1 \\ (1)-2(0)+(1) & =1 \\ 2 & =1\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $0\notin Π,$ this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement IV is true. Since statements II and III are false, $L$ is *not* a subspace of ${R}^{3}.$

17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Let $Π$ be the plane with equation $2x-y+z=2$ in ${R}^{3}.$ Which of the following statements are true? 
- **I.** $Π$ contains the zero-vector
- **II.** $Π$ is closed under vector addition
- **III.** $Π$ is closed under scalar multiplication
- **IV.** $Π$ is a subspace of ${R}^{3}$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

Notice that $Π$ contains vectors of the form 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ 2-2x+y\end{bmatrix},\,x,y\in R.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is false. The line does not pass through the origin since

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-y+z & =2 \\ 2(0)-(0)+(0) & =2 \\ 0 & =2\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Let's consider $a=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\in Π$ and $b=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\in Π.$ Then 

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0+0 \\ 0+(-2) \\ 2+0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

However, $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}$ does not belong to $Π$ since 

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-y+z & =2 \\ 2(0)-(-2)+(2) & =2 \\ 4 & =2\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $0\notin Π,$ this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement IV is false. Since statements II and III are false, $L$ is *not* a subspace of ${R}^{3}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true.""} {:db/id 17592186376068 :question/id #uuid "b6fdf40e-16e2-5d4d-87e5-0c2a5c46b067" :question/math-academy-id "q-157475" $$

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+2y+z & =1 \\ 3(1)+2(-1)+(1) & =1 \\ 2 & =1\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $0\notin Π,$ this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement IV is false. Since statements II and III are false, $L$ is *not* a subspace of ${R}^{3}.$

I. $Π$ contains the zero-vector

II. $Π$ is closed under vector addition

III. $Π$ is closed under scalar multiplication

IV. $Π$ is a subspace of ${R}^{3}$" :question/worked-solution "Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

Notice that $Π$ contains vectors of the form 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ 3x+2y\end{bmatrix},\,x,y\in R.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is true. The coordinates of the zero-vector satisfy the equation $z=3x+2y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =3x+2y \\ (0) & =3(0)+2(0) \\ 0 & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Let, for example, $a=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} \\ 3{a}_{1}+2{a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\in Π$ and $b=\begin{bmatrix}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2} \\ 3{b}_{1}+2{b}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\in Π.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} \\ 3{a}_{1}+2{a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2} \\ 3{b}_{1}+2{b}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1}+{b}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}+{b}_{2} \\ (3{a}_{1}+2{a}_{2})+(3{b}_{1}+2{b}_{2})\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1}+{b}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}+{b}_{2} \\ 3({a}_{1}+{b}_{1})+2({a}_{2}+{b}_{2})\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $z=3x+2y.$ Therefore, $a+b\in Π.$

- Statement III is true. Let, for example, $a=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} \\ 3{a}_{1}+2{a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\in Π$ and $k\in R.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}k\cdot a & =k\cdot \begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} \\ 3{a}_{1}+2{a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}k{a}_{1} \\ k{a}_{2} \\ k(3{a}_{1}+2{a}_{2})\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}k{a}_{1} \\ k{a}_{2} \\ 3k{a}_{1}+2k{a}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $z=3x+2y.$ Therefore, $k\cdot a\in Π.$

- Statement IV is true. Since statements II and III are true, the plane $Π$ must be a subspace of ${R}^{3}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "All the statements are true.""} {:db/id 17592186048337} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "24252954-787b-5287-ada3-c3c084627cbc" :answer/type {:db/id :topic/math-academy-id 1853} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186120884 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121126 :tutorial/content "A **subspace** of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a subset of $\mathbb R^n$ that is closed  under vector addition and scalar multiplication. In other words: 

$H\subseteq \mathbb R^n$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$ if and only if it satisfies the following properties:

- *Closure under vector addition:* 

$\qquad$ If $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are in $H,$ then their sum $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}$ is also in $H.$

- *Closure under scalar multiplication:* 

$\qquad$ If $\mathbf{u}$ is in $H,$ then $c\cdot \mathbf{u}$ is also in $H$ for any scalar number $c.$

For example, consider the line $L$ with equation $y=3x$ in $\mathbb{R}^2.$ Is $L$ a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2?$ 

First, notice that we can express the points on $L$ as the following set:

![](images/1f/1f380f9928da2dd44ff157a72fce97c02ae44626df515d52ece6ff5feee302d2.svg)

In other words, $L$ contains all vectors of the form ![](images/90/90996c2ffae29c3bd9cd3ab398cca4dd7e1b8fbe275de8520a72a16e504fb0f3.svg) where $x$ is a real number.

To determine whether $L$ is a subspace of $\mathbb R^2,$ we need to check the two conditions above. 

- Let's pick two arbitrary vectors in $L,$ namely, ![](images/59/59be22e80d0be32c84a8c2bdb2f2c96b23a0941d4aba26bdefa078fd299c137c.svg) and ![](images/d7/d78ea4fcfbd469e88b7fe46e28ac6f396a538c577f4defdd1b3d60e60df3c4b7.svg) If we compute their sum, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}u+v & =\begin{bmatrix}{u}_{1} \\ 3{u}_{1}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}{v}_{1} \\ 3{v}_{1}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{u}_{1}+{v}_{1} \\ 3{u}_{1}+3{v}_{1}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{u}_{1}+{v}_{1} \\ 3\cdot ({u}_{1}+{v}_{1})\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $y=3x.$ Therefore, $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v} \in L. \quad {\color{green}\checkmark}$

- Let's pick an arbitrary vector in $L,$ namely, ![](images/75/759c7883ad2772f20a090ad2f8c5dfe01031ca31e2b5f0e7681c945c9256c91d.svg) Then, for any scalar $c$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}c\cdot u & =c\cdot \begin{bmatrix}{u}_{1} \\ 3{u}_{1}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}c{u}_{1} \\ 3\cdot c{u}_{1}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $y=3x.$ Therefore, $c\cdot \mathbf{u}\in L. \quad {\color{green}\checkmark}$

The set $L$ satisfies both conditions. So, we can conclude that it is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2.$

**Note:** Since the second condition must be satisfied for any $c,$ including $c=0,$ we can conclude that every subspace must contain the zero vector $\mathbf{0}.$ So, if a set does not contain $\mathbf{0}$ then it is *not* a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n.$

For instance, the set 

![](images/a1/a15e0b4fc4544421e572d15b8fd016c3fa8721e0ecf3f8808a469c3252d1f6d6.svg)

does *not* contain the zero vector (since $0 \neq 0 + 1$), and consequently it is *not* a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ee2c580c-5386-5e06-9b58-e9e1dd398cd3" {:db/id 17592186120888 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121127 :tutorial/content "Recall that $H$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$ if and only if it satisfies the following properties:

*Closure under vector addition:* 

 $\qquad$ If $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are in $H,$ then their sum $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}$ is also in $H.$

*Closure under scalar multiplication:* 

 $\qquad$ If $\mathbf{u}$ is in $H,$ then $c\cdot \mathbf{u}$ is also in $H$ for any scalar number $c.$

Let $L$ be the line in $\mathbb{R}^3$ that passes through the points $(0,0,0)$ and $(4,1,-2).$ Is $L$ a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3?$ 

First, note that the direction vector of the line $L$ is 
![](images/25/25fa34994b33e0d11fd8990dddbfda276857e699018b4701c6e2eaf13acb0c20.svg)
This means that the vector equation of the line is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4t \\ t \\ -2t\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

for $t\in\mathbb R,$ and the corresponding Cartesian equation is 

$$
\dfrac x4=y=\dfrac z{-2}.
$$

To determine whether $L$ is a subspace, we need to check the two conditions above:

- Let's pick two arbitrary vectors in $L,$ namely, ![](images/d7/d7f1a3cf1625ff12bc96324dc428e1c95d271d8a72de603b671f722b9173281d.svg) and ![](images/25/255fc61225b017a51ae60b1d157787ac4b60fe596ebaa8296b48053b87b2eae7.svg) If we compute their sum, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}u+v & =\begin{bmatrix}4{u}_{1} \\ {u}_{1} \\ -2{u}_{1}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}4{v}_{1} \\ {v}_{1} \\ -2{v}_{1}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4{u}_{1}+4{v}_{1} \\ {u}_{1}+{v}_{1} \\ (-2{u}_{1})+(-2{v}_{1})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4\cdot ({u}_{1}+{v}_{1}) \\ {u}_{1}+{v}_{1} \\ (-2)\cdot ({u}_{1}+{v}_{1})\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $\dfrac x4=y=\dfrac z{-2}.$ Therefore, $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}\in L. \quad {\color{green}\checkmark}$

- Let's pick an arbitrary vector in $L,$ namely, ![](images/7f/7f7df4272eae1975b5802d54dfae499c528661ba0ae82faff45bb26f6cfab276.svg) Then, for any scalar $c,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}c\cdot u & =c\cdot \begin{bmatrix}4{u}_{1} \\ {u}_{1} \\ -2{u}_{1}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4\cdot c{u}_{1} \\ c{u}_{1} \\ (-2)\cdot c{u}_{1}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $\dfrac x4=y=\dfrac z{-2}.$ Therefore, $c\cdot \mathbf{u}\in L. \quad {\color{green}\checkmark}$

The set $L$ satisfies both conditions. So, we can conclude that it is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "fb0bb214-7f56-557a-82f7-baeef815457e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6859 :tutorial/title "Lines as Subspaces of Three-Dimensional Space"} :step/id #uuid "124c571f-28f0-56fa-a68d-76ef241f4618" :step/math-academy-id 41674 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120886}} {:db/id 17592186120889 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121128 :tutorial/content "Again, recall that $H$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$ if and only if it satisfies the following properties:

In other words: 

$H\subseteq \mathbb R^n$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$ if and only if it satisfies the following properties:

- *Closure under vector addition:* 

$\qquad$ If $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are in $H,$ then their sum $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}$ is also in $H.$

- *Closure under scalar multiplication:* 

$\qquad$ If $\mathbf{u}$ is in $H,$ then $c\cdot \mathbf{u}$ is also in $H$ for any scalar number $c.$

For example, consider the line $L$ with equation $y=3x$ in $\mathbb{R}^2.$ Is $L$ a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2?$ 

First, notice that we can express the points on $L$ as the following set:

![](images/1f/1f380f9928da2dd44ff157a72fce97c02ae44626df515d52ece6ff5feee302d2.svg)

In other words, $L$ contains all vectors of the form ![](images/90/90996c2ffae29c3bd9cd3ab398cca4dd7e1b8fbe275de8520a72a16e504fb0f3.svg) where $x$ is a real number.

To determine whether $L$ is a subspace of $\mathbb R^2,$ we need to check the two conditions above. 

- Let's pick two arbitrary vectors in $L,$ namely, ![](images/59/59be22e80d0be32c84a8c2bdb2f2c96b23a0941d4aba26bdefa078fd299c137c.svg) and ![](images/d7/d78ea4fcfbd469e88b7fe46e28ac6f396a538c577f4defdd1b3d60e60df3c4b7.svg) If we compute their sum, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}u+v & =\begin{bmatrix}{u}_{1} \\ 3{u}_{1}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}{v}_{1} \\ 3{v}_{1}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{u}_{1}+{v}_{1} \\ 3{u}_{1}+3{v}_{1}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{u}_{1}+{v}_{1} \\ 3\cdot ({u}_{1}+{v}_{1})\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $y=3x.$ Therefore, $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v} \in L. \quad {\color{green}\checkmark}$

- Let's pick an arbitrary vector in $L,$ namely, ![](images/75/759c7883ad2772f20a090ad2f8c5dfe01031ca31e2b5f0e7681c945c9256c91d.svg) Then, for any scalar $c$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}c\cdot u & =c\cdot \begin{bmatrix}{u}_{1} \\ 3{u}_{1}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}c{u}_{1} \\ 3\cdot c{u}_{1}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $y=3x.$ Therefore, $c\cdot \mathbf{u}\in L. \quad {\color{green}\checkmark}$

The set $L$ satisfies both conditions. So, we can conclude that it is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2.$

**Note:** Since the second condition must be satisfied for any $c,$ including $c=0,$ we can conclude that every subspace must contain the zero vector $\mathbf{0}.$ So, if a set does not contain $\mathbf{0}$ then it is *not* a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n.$

For instance, the set 

![](images/a1/a15e0b4fc4544421e572d15b8fd016c3fa8721e0ecf3f8808a469c3252d1f6d6.svg)

does *not* contain the zero vector (since $0 \neq 0 + 1$), and consequently it is *not* a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ee2c580c-5386-5e06-9b58-e9e1dd398cd3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6853 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "7f009ee8-4a5e-5da7-b539-b2991cbd9d04" :step/math-academy-id 41645 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120885}} {:db/id 17592186121126 :tutorial/content "A **subspace** of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a subset of $\mathbb R^n$ that is closed  under vector addition and scalar multiplication. $$

- Let's pick two arbitrary vectors in $L,$ namely, ![](images/d7/d7f1a3cf1625ff12bc96324dc428e1c95d271d8a72de603b671f722b9173281d.svg) and ![](images/25/255fc61225b017a51ae60b1d157787ac4b60fe596ebaa8296b48053b87b2eae7.svg) If we compute their sum, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}c\cdot u & =c\cdot \begin{bmatrix}4{u}_{1} \\ {u}_{1} \\ -2{u}_{1}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4\cdot c{u}_{1} \\ c{u}_{1} \\ (-2)\cdot c{u}_{1}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $\dfrac x4=y=\dfrac z{-2}.$ Therefore, $c\cdot \mathbf{u}\in L. \quad {\color{green}\checkmark}$

:question/math-academy-id "q-157377" :question/problem "Let $L$ be the line in ${R}^{3}$ that passes through the points $(1,1,1)$ and $(2,-1,2).$ Which of the following statements are true?
- **I.** $L$ contains the zero-vector
- **II.** $L$ is closed under vector addition
- **III.** $L$ is closed under scalar multiplication
- **IV.** $L$ is a subspace of ${R}^{3}$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is false. The direction vector of the line $L$ is 

$$
d=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

This means that the vector equation of the line is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

for $t\in R,$ and the corresponding Cartesian equation is 

$$
x-1=\frac{y-1}{-2}=z-1.
$$

But this line does not pass through the origin since 

$$
(0)-1\ne \frac{(0)-1}{-2}\ne (0)-1.\,\times 
$$

- Statement II is false. Let's consider the vectors $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ and $\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}$ from $L$ (the position vectors of the given points). Then,

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

However, the point $(3,0,3)$ does not belong to $L$ since

$$
(3)-1\ne \frac{(0)-1}{-2}\ne (3)-1.\,\times 
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $0\notin L,$ this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement IV is false. Since statements II and III are false, $L$ is *not* a subspace of ${R}^{3}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true.""} :step/id #uuid "1436249c-5de8-51a2-9062-17b0c4a22818" :step/next {:db/id 17592186417224}} {:db/id 17592186417221 :step/content :question/math-academy-id "q-157374" :question/problem "Let $L$ be the line in ${R}^{3}$ that passes through the points $(0,0,0)$ and $(1,-2,3).$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $L$ contains the zero-vector

- **II.** $L$ is closed under vector addition

- **III.** $L$ is closed under scalar multiplication

- **IV.** $L$ is a subspace of ${R}^{3}$" :question/worked-solution "Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

First, note that the direction vector of the line $L$ is 

$$
d=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

This means that the vector equation of the line is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}t \\ -2t \\ 3t\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

for $t\in R,$ and the corresponding Cartesian equation is 

$$
x=-\frac{y}{2}=\frac{z}{3}.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is true. Indeed, from the definition of $L$ we have that the point $(0,0,0)$ is in $L.$

- Statement II is true. Let, for example, $a=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ -2a \\ 3a\end{bmatrix}\in L$ and $b=\begin{bmatrix}b \\ -2b \\ 3b\end{bmatrix}\in L.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =\begin{bmatrix}a \\ -2a \\ 3a\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}b \\ -2b \\ 3b\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}a+b \\ (-2a)+(-2b) \\ 3a+3b\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}a+b \\ -2(a+b) \\ 3(a+b)\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the conditions $x=-\frac{y}{2}=\frac{z}{3}.$ Therefore, $a+b\in L.$

- Statement III is true. Let, for example, $a=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ -2a \\ 3a\end{bmatrix}\in L$ and $k\in R.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}k\cdot a & =k\cdot \begin{bmatrix}a \\ -2a \\ 3a\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}ka \\ k(-2a) \\ k(3a)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}ka \\ -2(ka) \\ 3(ka)\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the conditions $x=-\frac{y}{2}=\frac{z}{3}.$ Therefore, $k\cdot a\in L.$

- Statement IV is true. Since statements II and III are true, $L$ is a subspace of ${R}^{3}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "All the statements are true.""} :step/id #uuid "1821a5bc-a723-5459-b893-12f5b2f84d53" :step/next {:db/id 17592186417220}} {:db/id 17592186417222 :step/content {:db/id - If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

$$
\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ x-y-1\end{bmatrix},\,x,y\in R.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =x-y-1 \\ (0) & =(0)-(0)-(1) \\ 0 & =-1\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

However, $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}$ does not belong to $Π$ since 

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =x-y-1 \\ (-1) & =(1)-(0)-1 \\ -1 & =0\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $0\notin Π,$ this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement IV is true. Since statements II and III are false, $L$ is *not* a subspace of ${R}^{3}.$

:question/math-academy-id "q-157476" :question/problem "Let $Π$ be the plane with equation $x-2y+2z=3$ in ${R}^{3}.$ Which of the following statements are true? 

I. $Π$ contains the zero-vector

II. $Π$ is closed under vector addition

III. $Π$ is closed under scalar multiplication

IV. $Π$ is a subspace of ${R}^{3}$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

Notice that $Π$ contains vectors of the form 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3+2y-2z \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix},\,y,z\in R.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is false. The line does not pass through the origin since

$$
\begin{aligned}x-2y+2z & =3 \\ (0)-2(0)+2(0) & =3 \\ 0 & =3\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Let's consider $a=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\in Π$ and $b=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\in Π.$ Then 

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3+1 \\ 0+0 \\ 0+1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

However, $\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ does not belong to $Π$ since 

$$
\begin{aligned}x-2y+2z & =3 \\ (4)-2(0)+2(1) & =3 \\ 6 & =3\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $0\notin Π,$ this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement IV is false. Since statements II and III are false, $L$ is *not* a subspace of ${R}^{3}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true.""} :step/id #uuid "f20bfc1c-6733-50b5-9d02-7dbeed933bee"}] :activity/title "Subspaces of N-Dimensional Space" :activity/type {:db/id :question/math-academy-id "q-156620" :question/problem "Let $L$ be the line with equation $4x=2y$ in ${R}^{2}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $L$ contains the zero-vector
- **II.** $L$ is closed under vector addition
- **III.** $L$ is closed under scalar multiplication
- **IV.** $L$ is **not** a subspace of ${R}^{2}$" :question/worked-solution "Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

Notice that $L$ contains vectors of the form 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ 2x\end{bmatrix},\,x\in R.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is true. The coordinates of the zero-vector satisfy the equation $4x=2y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4x & =2y \\ 4(0) & =2(0) \\ 0 & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Let, for example, $a=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 2a\end{bmatrix}\in L$ and $b=\begin{bmatrix}b \\ 2b\end{bmatrix}\in L.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 2a\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}b \\ 2b\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}a+b \\ 2a+2b\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}a+b \\ 2(a+b)\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the condition $4x=2y.$ Therefore, $a+b\in L.$

- Statement III is true. Let, for example, $a=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 2a\end{bmatrix}\in L$ and $k\in R.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}k\cdot a & =k\cdot \begin{bmatrix}a \\ 2a\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}ka \\ k(2a)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}ka \\ 2(ka)\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

 
which satisfies the condition $4x=2y.$ Therefore, $k\cdot a\in L.$

- Statement IV is false. Since statements II and III are true, $L$ must be a subspace of ${R}^{2}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III only.""} :step/id #uuid "a6b1b4f4-42fd-518f-9611-64b9f9fd951d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186417222}} {:db/id 17592186417220 :step/content {:db/id :question/math-academy-id "q-157377" :question/problem "Let $L$ be the line in ${R}^{3}$ that passes through the points $(1,1,1)$ and $(2,-1,2).$ Which of the following statements are true?
- **I.** $L$ contains the zero-vector
- **II.** $L$ is closed under vector addition
- **III.** $L$ is closed under scalar multiplication
- **IV.** $L$ is a subspace of ${R}^{3}$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is false. The direction vector of the line $L$ is 

$$
d=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

This means that the vector equation of the line is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

for $t\in R,$ and the corresponding Cartesian equation is 

$$
x-1=\frac{y-1}{-2}=z-1.
$$

But this line does not pass through the origin since 

$$
(0)-1\ne \frac{(0)-1}{-2}\ne (0)-1.\,\times 
$$

- Statement II is false. Let's consider the vectors $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ and $\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}$ from $L$ (the position vectors of the given points). Then,

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

However, the point $(3,0,3)$ does not belong to $L$ since

$$
(3)-1\ne \frac{(0)-1}{-2}\ne (3)-1.\,\times 
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $0\notin L,$ this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement IV is false. Since statements II and III are false, $L$ is *not* a subspace of ${R}^{3}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true.""} :step/id #uuid "1436249c-5de8-51a2-9062-17b0c4a22818" :step/next {:db/id 17592186417224}} {:db/id 17592186417224 :step/content - If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

First, note that the direction vector of the line $L$ is 

$$
d=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

This means that the vector equation of the line is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}t \\ -2t \\ 3t\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

for $t\in R,$ and the corresponding Cartesian equation is 

$$
x=-\frac{y}{2}=\frac{z}{3}.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is true. Indeed, from the definition of $L$ we have that the point $(0,0,0)$ is in $L.$

- Statement II is true. Let, for example, $a=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ -2a \\ 3a\end{bmatrix}\in L$ and $b=\begin{bmatrix}b \\ -2b \\ 3b\end{bmatrix}\in L.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =\begin{bmatrix}a \\ -2a \\ 3a\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}b \\ -2b \\ 3b\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}a+b \\ (-2a)+(-2b) \\ 3a+3b\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}a+b \\ -2(a+b) \\ 3(a+b)\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the conditions $x=-\frac{y}{2}=\frac{z}{3}.$ Therefore, $a+b\in L.$

- Statement III is true. Let, for example, $a=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ -2a \\ 3a\end{bmatrix}\in L$ and $k\in R.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}k\cdot a & =k\cdot \begin{bmatrix}a \\ -2a \\ 3a\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}ka \\ k(-2a) \\ k(3a)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}ka \\ -2(ka) \\ 3(ka)\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the conditions $x=-\frac{y}{2}=\frac{z}{3}.$ Therefore, $k\cdot a\in L.$

- Statement IV is true. Since statements II and III are true, $L$ is a subspace of ${R}^{3}.$
